rows.evidence: Q1: Methods and Results sections (Tables 1-3, Figs 3-11) report the authors' own HSPF model runs for the Tumenxigou catchment driven by five bias-corrected GCMs under RCP 8.5, with calibration/validation against 2014-2015 observations.
rows.notes: The study contains no remote sensing: soil moisture is an output of the HSPF watershed model, not a satellite surface soil moisture retrieval, and no SSM-to-RZSM transformation is performed. It reports projected changes in runoff, ET, sediment, TN, TP and fecal coliform loads under drought/rainfall patterns; it does not examine crop yield or crop yield forecasting at all. The claim's technology (remote-sensing SSM) and effect (crop yield forecasting) are both absent, so the study provides no evidence of its own on the claim.

rows.evidence: Q1: Methods and Results sections (Tables 1-3, Figs 3-11) report the authors' own HSPF model simulations for the Tumenxigou catchment under five GCMs (RCP 8.5), calibrated and validated against observed streamflow and water quality data.
rows.notes: The study does not use remote sensing products of any kind; soil water content is simulated by the HSPF model. Its own result is that heavy rain and rainstorm events following prolonged drought, modulated by antecedent soil water, increase runoff, sediment, nutrient and fecal coliform export in a drinking-water source catchment, and it recommends that adaptive watershed management focus on these events. It does not evaluate remote-sensing SSM retrieval or its contribution to climate-resilient agricultural management, so there is no own evidence on the claimed technology or effect.

notes: Full text appears complete (abstract through references). The study is a watershed hydrology/water-quality modeling study (HSPF + GCM projections) with no remote-sensing component; it is cited by the review alongside others for a forward-looking statement about SSM retrieval applications, which this study does not address.
